NAS100 9:30 Hedge Study · 2020–2026

The idea: at the 9:30 New York open, buy and sell the same size at the same time. Wait for a move of X points either way, bank the leg in profit (half or all), then manage what's left on a continuation or a reversal. Data: 1,475 trading days (2020-07 → 2026-10) of 1-minute MNQ as the NAS100 stand-in; NQ futures points ≈ NAS100 index points. One setup per day. Results are in points per 1 lot on each leg. Most brokers' NAS100 / USTEC 1 lot = $1 a point, so 0.1 lot = $0.10 a point; check yours. Costs: the spread is paid once per leg (1.5 points by default; 0, 1.0 and 2.5 shown too), no commission (standard account). Inside a minute the path is open → the low then the high on an up-minute (the high then the low on a down-minute) → close. 987 rule sets were tested, so single top rows are flattered by selection; trust the families and the 2020–23 vs 2024–26 split.

Why the hedge as you described it loses

A buy and a sell of the same size cancel out: until something is closed, the account just pays two spreads and moves nowhere. Everything happens at the first exit. When the leg in profit is closed at +X, what stays open is the losing leg, a position against the move (plus any part of the winner you kept). From that moment the "hedge" is a directional trade that bets the move will come back.

So the rules you described (bank the winner at +100, then wait for a reversal to get the loser out) are a fade of the first 100-point move after the open. On NAS100 after 9:30 that move tends to continue more often than it reverses, so the fade loses. Every one of the 735 hedge variants that keep the losing leg (any X, half or all banked, breakeven or ½X reversal exits, loser stops at 1.5–2X, trailing, close at net +) lost money in at least one half.

Flip it: cut the losing leg at −X and let the winner run, and the same straddle becomes a breakout trade that rides the continuation. That's the side with the edge. It's the same as placing a buy stop and a sell stop X away (an OCO breakout), except the hedge pays one extra spread for the leg you cut. The table below shows both, and they match.
